title: How Rocky Became the Heart of Philadelphia
full_text: × Skip to main content Cover Story Alix Earle Bares All: How the TikToker Is Becoming Beauty’s Next Billion-Dollar Mogul close By Zach Goins Plus Icon Zach Goins View All November 18, 2026 9:47am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Sylvester Stallone as Rocky Balboa celebrating at the top of the Philadelphia Museum of Art stairs Image Courtesy of Amazon MGM Studios Every year, visitors from around the world make the pilgrimage to the Philadelphia Museum of Art , where 72 stone steps have become one of cinema’s most recognizable landmarks. Many come not for artwork, but to recreate Rocky Balboa’s triumphant ascent, arms raised above the city that made him a legend. But when Sylvester Stallone first raced up those steps in 1976, Philadelphia was a far cry from the tourist destination immortalized on screen. At the time, the city was struggling economically, with its aging neighborhoods and industrial character reflecting the hardships faced by many of its residents. Rather than shy away from those realities, the filmmakers embraced them. Related Stories Movies The Underdog Story Behind the Underdog Story Movies 'Godzilla Minus Zero' Powers $31M in Historic Box Office Launch Against Subdued 'Cat in the Hat' “We very much wanted to show the city as it was from the viewpoint of Rocky, from the viewpoint of a working-class guy,” producer Irwin Winkler said. From the rowhouses and neighborhood streets of South Philadelphia to the modest pet shop where Adrian worked, Rocky captured a community of ordinary people trying to make ends meet. Rocky collected debts for a loan shark, Adrian struggled with her confidence, and Paulie was rough around the edges, but beneath their imperfections were characters whose humanity made them relatable, Winkler recalled. One of the film’s most enduring images wasn’t even part of the original screenplay, according to I Play Rocky director Peter Farrelly . With the production operating on a limited budget, the filmmakers relied heavily on the newly developed Steadicam , invented the year prior by cinematographer Garrett Brown . The Steadicam allowed filmmakers to follow moving subjects with unprecedented freedom, and Rocky director John G. Avildsen recruited Brown to operate his new invention for the now iconic “Rocky Steps” sequence. The result transformed a simple training run into a universal image of triumph, with Rocky reaching the top of the steps and raising his arms toward the Philadelphia skyline. Sylvester Stallone and cinematographer and inventor Garrett Brown operating the newly invented Steadicam Image Courtesy of Amazon MGM Studios Five decades later, the steps remain a destination for generations of moviegoers, while Rocky Balboa has become one of Philadelphia’s most enduring cultural ambassadors—a fictional underdog whose determination and resilience have come to embody the city’s working-class spirit. title: From Book Club to Netflix: How Katherine Center’s ‘The Bodyguard’ Became ‘Guarding Stars’
full_text: × Skip to main content Cover Story Alix Earle Bares All: How the TikToker Is Becoming Beauty’s Next Billion-Dollar Mogul close From left: ‘The Bodyguard’ by Katherine Center book cover; A still from Netflix’s ‘Guarding Stars’ film. St. Martin's Press; Netflix Some stories refuse to stay on the page. The Hollywood Reporter’ s Beyond the Book column explores what happens when books make the leap to screen and beyond — unpacking what stayed, changed, how it was done and why it matters with the creatives who made it. *** When director Liz Allen Rosenbaum first scrolled through BookTok, she had an epiphany. The Purple Hearts director, whose credits also include Aquamarine, the upcoming Aquamarine pilot for Disney and Ramona and Beezus, kept finding fan-made lists of the romance tropes readers love most: enemies to lovers, forced proximity and only one bed. She recognized some from her own work. Related Stories Business New York Knicks Star Josh Hart Inks Two-Book Deal With HarperCollins (Exclusive) Movies Lee Chang-dong on the Mysteries and Meaning of 'Possible Love' “Oh my God, I’ve been called out. I’m a cliché,” she remembers thinking. Then she started taking notes. By the time she was developing the Netflix romance film Guarding Stars , those notes had become a working checklist. “Any time there wasn’t enough enemies-to-lovers in the script, I’d say, ‘We need more enemy here! Where’s the enemy?’” Rosenbaum tells The Hollywood Reporter . Those notes and being attuned to what fans of the book and romance readers want ended up shaping her new film Guarding Stars , Netflix’s adaptation of Katherine Center’s 2022 novel The Bodyguard , which premieres on the streamer on Nov. 18. Leighton Meester stars as Hannah Brooks, a bodyguard assigned to protect movie star Jack Stapleton ( Jared Padalecki ) and ends up posing as his girlfriend while staying with him at his family’s Montana ranch over the holidays. But just as readers were top of mind for Rosenbaum, the film’s road to the screen started with that audience too. Producer Genevieve Padalecki selected Center‘s book for her Instagram book club, which led to an Instagram Live with the author and, months later, an option. As studios and streamers turn to romance novels for their built-in audiences, the people who made Guarding Stars say they kept Center’s fans in mind at every step, from the script to the Easter eggs. In separate conversations with THR , members of the creative team behind the film detail how the new holiday romance came together. “She Loves Stories” Author Katherine Center and Genevieve Padelecki first bonded after Padelecki selected The Bodyguard as her online book club pick. The kinship led to interest in adapting it. KATHERINE CENTER (AUTHOR): Gen got in touch and said she wanted to feature The Bodyguard in her online book club. Back then it was just Instagram. Of course I said yes, and we did an Instagram Live together, and I instantly fell madly in love with Genevieve Padalecki, because she’s a book person. She had the best possible book-person, English-major energy. When you’re a writer and you talk to a lot of readers, you can tell when somebody genuinely loves books for all the right reasons, people who just love getting lost in stories. The minute I met her, I thought, “Oh, she loves stories.” I could have gone for 10 hours. I thought that would be that. What a lovely treat. Then, maybe six months later they circled back about wanting to option it. I said, yes, please, no pressure. And I don’t know how we got here, but here we are. GENEVIEVE PADALECKI (PRODUCER): One thing I love about Katherine’s books is that they have strong female leads who aren’t wilting flowers. They’re women with a struggle, a backstory. They’re not crippled by the chips in their armor; it actually reinforces them. And then on top of that, you have the flip side of the bodyguard story: a tiny, petite, Lilliputian female bodyguard guarding a male celebrity. I immediately thought, this would be so fun for Jared [Padalecki]. The book has all the wonderful tropes we love in a rom-com, the things we come back to and watch on repeat. So I turned to Jared and said, “We have to find a way to partner with Katherine and bring this to life.” “We Have to Do This Movie!” After finding a home at Netflix, a team was assembled including director Liz Allen Rosenbaum and producers and co-writers Gina Matthews, Grant Scharbo, Erin Cardillo and Richard Keith. From left: Director Liz Allen, Jared Padalecki as Jack and Andie MacDowell as Connie on the set of Guarding Stars. Chris Large/Netflix PADALECKI: When we came to Netflix with this story, they got it immediately. They loved this story so much, and it just became a natural fit. GINA MATTHEWS (PRODUCER/CO-WRITER): Netflix reached out to us [herself and producer-husband Grant Scharbo] when they were considering the book. Jared and Gen had brought it to them, and they were looking for people who had produced and written a lot in the rom-com and holiday space, because Gen and Jared were new to that as producers. I produced What Women Want , 13 Going on 30 and Isn’t It Romantic . It’s a genre that’s really close to our hearts, and it’s hard to do well. We loved Katherine’s book because of the way she writes characters, and she’s not afraid to go to emotional places. It’s funny, and it’s high-concept; it has everything that makes a book a solid, strong movie adaptation. But what we also loved is that there’s real heart and real trauma these characters have to get over on this journey, inside a big, fun holiday romantic comedy with action. We love movies that take audiences on that ride, where you’re laughing, and then you’re crying, and you’re like, “Oh my God, I was literally laughing 20 minutes ago, and now I’m in tears.” RICHARD KEITH (PRODUCER/CO-WRITER): Gina sent it to us [himself and producer/co-writer] Erin Cardillo] to see if we were interested. I put the audiobook on [while] leaving L.A., and about two hours in, I had to pull over to charge the car. I texted Gina: “Oh my God, we have to do this movie. I’m obsessed with this book!“ Erin and I are both huge fans of old-school, Richard Curtis-style rom-coms, and there are very few where the two leads get to spend most of the movie together. ERIN CARDILLO (PRODUCER/CO-WRITER): I just loved it! She’s a delightful writer: whimsical and funny, with characters so specifically drawn. We both fell in love with it. LIZ ALLEN ROSENBAUM (DIRECTOR): It came to me as a director-for-hire project, and I’d been really choosy about those, because I was developing my own material. But my agent said, “It’s a go movie. You should really take it seriously.” So I read it, and the moment Hannah flips Jack on that tarmac, I thought, “Oh! I’ve actually never seen anything like this” where the woman was the strong one. I’ve only done female-oriented projects my whole career, and I’d never seen anything where the woman was the strong one. I had to put everything else aside for a minute and make this. “Everybody Shared the Same North Star” — Putting Readers First With a built-in audience already for Center’s bestseller, the creative team always had readers at top of mind when sorting out how to bring it to life onscreen. From left: Center and producer Gina Matthews on the Guarding Stars set. Chris Large/Netflix ROSENBAUM: Believe it or not, almost every movie and pilot I’ve done has been based on a book. But Purple Hearts [which Rosenbaum directed] came as BookTok was taking off, and I wasn’t really acquainted with it. It had a very small budget and no big marketing campaign, and when it started to take off, I was like, “What’s happening?” We knocked The Gray Man , a $200 million movie, right off the top spot, and it was because of that grassroots groundswell of well-read, cool women. So I started spending all this time on BookTok accounts, trying to understand it. They kept talking about tropes, and I grew up thinking those were bad. They make lists of the tropes they love [including] “enemies to lovers,“ “there’s only one bed“ and you’ve got to have “forced proximity.“ These are all words I’ve learned. The first time I said one, I’d have died of embarrassment: “Oh my God, I’ve been called out. I’m a cliché.” But then I started taking notes. And I realized tropes are good, and I love tropes! So on Guarding Stars , any time there wasn’t enough enemies-to-lovers in the script, I’d say, “We need more enemy here! Where’s the enemy?” We did a few drafts after I came on board, and there are plenty of things in this movie that I learned from what people enjoy and want. I’m feeding off the audience too, and I love them. MATTHEWS: We love that enemies-to-lovers trope. We really do. That conflict, getting under each other’s skin, is one of our most fun things to write. MATTHEWS: For Gen, with her book club, she really knows the emotional core of what’s going to resonate with those fans. And ironically, those fans are movie fans. Book fans and movie fans are the same in this genre. PADALECKI: Katherine’s fans in the book world are akin to the Supernatural fans. She has a very loud, excited audience. What was so fun was making sure we reached out to that audience. We did a thing about the title, and we made sure there were Easter eggs throughout that are very important to the story. Katherine’s input in keeping us on track was integral to making this film. GRANT SCHARBO (PRODUCER/CO-WRITER): Having a built-in audience definitely does not make it easier. You have this fear of disappointment. MATTHEWS: Everybody shared the same North Star: What are the most important things in the book that Katherine’s readers care about? The parts you found so emotional you cried? Or the part where she flips him at the opening of the movie, which is in the trailer? We wanted to keep those touchstones, especially because we weren’t able to use the title The Bodyguard . Of course we all wanted to, but there’s only one Bodyguard movie! ROSENBAUM: Katherine knows her audience so well. I don’t just mean psychologically. I mean she actually knows them. She makes a point of it and does so many things in person. Jared and Genevieve do that too. It’s this cyclical, beautiful circle that keeps feeding itself. And Katherine guided me through that. She knows what readers love about her book, and it’s been really helpful to have her blessing and her guidance. “They Brought Those Scenes to Life” Casting Jared Padalecki, “a rat-a-tat-tat, Bogart-and-Bacall romantic lead, “ and Leighton Meester, the “rom-com heroine we’ve all been waiting for” as the film’s leads. Jared Padalecki as Jack and Leighton Meester as Hannah. Netflix PADALECKI: I said, “Jared, you have to read this book. It’s so fun.” At the time he was filming Walker ; we were juggling three kids, and we were just coming out of the pandemic. He read it and was so excited. I don’t want to speak for him, but I think initially he was a little nervous. He’d never played a very confident, swaggering character like Jack Stapleton. But he was a pretty easy sell. ROSENBAUM: Jared was already attached when I came on board. It felt like a perfect fit. Before I signed on the dotted line, I watched a lot of his material. What hooked me was all his behind-the-scenes footage, because his character on Supernatural wasn’t a flirty, bantery character. But there’s an enormous amount of BTS on the internet with his co-star, and they’re so funny together. He’s a born rat-a-tat-tat, Bogart-and-Bacall romantic lead. I mean, part of the reason he hadn’t done a movie in a long time is because he’d been so busy and sought after for 20-some-odd years. I mean, who has that streak? He happened to be available. I was like, this is just perfect. CENTER: Jared Padalecki was born to play Jack! He totally nailed everything about that character. And can I also say he should just be in every rom-com ever? KEITH: He was instrumental in the development of the script. He and Gen loved the book, and he was adamant that we stay true to who Jack was. But in the book, Jack is pretty wonderful. His flaws are few and far between. To Jared’s credit, and some actors shy away from this, he really wanted to find some flaws in this man so we could give him room to grow. It was awesome to see him do that, especially in the scenes with Noah LaLonde. They’re really moving. The love story between the two brothers is just as integral to the plot as the love story between Leighton and Jared’s characters. MATTHEWS: Jared had a lot to do, because Jack is kind of a jerk. It’s the same as Mel Gibson in What Women Want . He could get away with so much because he was so charming. You’re like, “I want to smack you, but I kind of want to kiss you!“ “Jared Padalecki was born to play Jack,“ says Center. Netflix ROSENBAUM: Leighton’s a queen. She doesn’t have to audition anymore. I’d worked with her on Gossip Girl , just one episode, way back when it was getting started, but you learn enough in a few weeks to see the depth of somebody. She was so sharp with her comedy as Blair Waldorf. And apparently she had made a wish, or a New Year’s resolution, that action comedy would come her way, and then we sent her the script. CARDILLO: When her name came up in the casting process, we were both like, “Oh my God, yes, that would be so great.” She’s unsuspecting as a bodyguard. You don’t think of her that way, but she really is tough in this movie, and it’s something we haven’t seen her do before. KEITH: It needs to be someone unassuming enough to be Jared’s bodyguard without the parents suspecting but with that innate strength. I’d like to think we wrote a lot of funny lines for her, but she was never playing at being a bodyguard. She never acted like she was aware of the jokes. PADALECKI: I remember in some of our first meetings, her descriptions of how she saw the characters brought so much depth and humor that I didn’t even know was in Hannah. She’s truly one of the hardest-working humans I’ve ever met. “She’s truly one of the hardest-working humans I’ve ever met,“ Gen Padalecki says of Leighton Meester. Chris Large/Netflix CENTER: She’s the rom-com heroine we’ve all been waiting for. She does this perfect balance of tough but vulnerable. You want somebody you can admire, with a lot of moxie. But I also want her to break my heart a little bit. Yes, in real life she’s a movie star. But in this movie, she’s me. She can take Jared Padalecki and flip him over like that, but there are also things that scare her. MATTHEWS: You can write that crackle on the page, but you don’t know how it’s going to be. Neither of them comes at it from a place that feels false or disingenuous. It was really about character for both of them, and they brought those scenes to life in a way we couldn’t have dreamed of. “A Hug in Story Form” The team shifted the story to become a holiday film that serves as a “love story to families.” From left: Meester as Hannah and Padalecki as Jack. Netflix SCHARBO: We made it a Christmas movie. In the book, it was Thanksgiving. It’s a beloved book, and we know we have to make changes to adapt it, so it’s a lot of pressure to adapt something people love. We ran a lot of things by Katherine. “How do you feel about this?” And she would say, “I think they’ll be OK with that.” CENTER: My books are emotionally cozy. I want them to feel like a hug in story form. When you’re telling a story in visuals, and you have the contrast between very cold, snowy stuff outside and fireplaces and twinkle lights and candles inside, it helps you tell that story. This is a story about people who are out in the cold at the start, and then they find a way to reconnect with their families and themselves. You don’t just understand it intellectually; you feel it. CARDILLO: The book takes place over a longer period, and for a feature, condensing the time frame made a lot of sense. It makes it a little bigger for a movie, more fun to play with those holiday tropes. The stakes of spending Christmas with your family, versus just a stretch of time with them, were really appealing. KEITH: In movies, you want those scenes where you go, “Here’s where the movie really starts.” Andie MacDowell lying in a bed saying, “Well, you guys are going to stay for Christmas, right?” is such a concrete way into the concept that it was a no-brainer. ROSENBAUM: The story is really a love story to families. [Hannah]’s not only falling in love with [Jack]; she’s falling in love with the family, and she never knew she needed that. With movies, you have to turbocharge things. To me, Christmas is everything family is about. It’s the one time a year I see my whole extended family. You need a bigger holiday, where everybody’s home, people fly in and there’s magic. When I came on board, I had a big meeting with Netflix about making it even more about family. KEITH: We really loved the parents’ relationship being aspirational for the two leads. It has obviously informed the sons’ opinions of what love should be, but we wanted that for Leighton’s character as well. She grew up with a broken picture of what love could or should be. We really loved that in the book she’s not just falling in love with this guy, but with this family, and with the understanding that she deserves to be loved. It’s a love story on many levels. “This Is Better Than the Book” Slight creative liberties were taken when adapting the book, in particular with the family dynamic. One change even made the author prefer it over her original take. “I have no beef with my own scene. But the movie makes so much more of that moment,“ Center says of Jared Padalecki’s helicopter scene. Netflix PADALECKI: This is Katherine’s baby. She worked on this for a long time to put these words, these ideas and these characters onto the page. As a producer, taking it into a new medium, where we have to take the scalpel and dissect it and put it back together, means making sure the integrity is still there and that we’re honoring Katherine’s words. MATTHEWS: In the book, Hank is the older brother, but in the movie he’s Jack’s younger brother. And there were no kids in the book. That came when Liz came on. She thought there should be a family that represents the life Jack didn’t have. If it’s a younger brother who got left behind, there’s such an emotional feeling of abandonment. Hank is still angry. He still has all this resentment. But it’s grounded in feeling abandoned by the brother who should have been there to take care of him. I think fans will understand why and feel it’s a layered choice that still stays true to the book. We also wanted to see [Hannah] do her job. In the book, once they got to the ranch, they mostly stayed there, and it was about the relationship. She’s a female bodyguard who is underestimated by everyone. No one sees her coming, which is her superpower. So we asked, how can we create sequences that are cinematic and show her doing her job? At our test screenings, people who had read the book loved that. They got to see it in action and connected to her character even more. CENTER: The moment when Jared Padalecki gets out of the helicopter is not in the book. This is better than the book. In the book, she meets him at the house he’s renting, and it’s fine. I have no beef with my own scene. But the movie makes so much more of that moment: he’s getting out of a helicopter, he’s got aviators on, slow motion through the snow. I’m like, “This is so much better!” “A Family Event in Every Way” During filming, the cast’s families were always present with even Padalecki ‘s son acting in a scene while Walker Hayes’ wife was present for an onscreen kiss. Leighton Meester and Jared Padalecki Chris Large/Netflix ROSENBAUM: For about four months of prep, Jared and Gen were in every Zoom meeting. I was up in Calgary and they were in Austin, working out of their house, so I got to know their family. The kids would pop in and say hi. I thought, this movie’s about family, so you need your whole family in it. One of his sons plays the young version of him. He auditioned, because I didn’t want to put someone in who’d flounder, and he did a fantastic job! Jared had a grueling schedule, and it was so cold, and he stayed the whole time his son was shooting. In one scene, with the safety rules for little kids, it was Gen’s hands in an oven mitt, puppeteering it as if they were the kids’ hands. It was a family event in every way. Walker Hayes had auditioned for Hank. All of his kids helped him with that audition, giving him notes offscreen. I thought, “He’s interested in acting. Why don’t I make him the sheriff?“ The sheriff was written as about 65, and everyone said, “We can’t have a singing hot sheriff.” Yes, we can! [Hayes] and his wife met doing Little Shop of Horrors in high school, and the sheriff is supposed to kiss someone for the kiss cam. He said, “I can’t kiss anyone unless it’s my wife.” We had to appeal to the Canadian government to fly her up. It’s their onscreen debut together. “All of his kids helped him with that audition, giving him notes offscreen,“ Rosenbaum says of Walker Hayes auditioning for the film. Chris Large/Netflix CENTER: My novel-writing life is very isolated. I drive down to Galveston Island and spend four or five days alone with my imaginary friends. It’s me and the dog. So when I visited the set, I was blinking back tears the whole time, because everywhere I went there were people 100 percent invested in this story. Their whole month was about how to bring it to life, and the project just happened to be my book. I got to take my mother, and we spent a full day bebopping around the set. I’m the middle of three girls, and we’re always in a light competition over who our mother loves most. I got some street cred in that fight that I may never have to give up. “She [Rosenbaum] thought there should be a family that represents the life Jack didn’t have. If it’s a younger brother who got left behind, there’s such an emotional feeling of abandonment,” says Matthews of Noah LaLonde portraying Jack‘s younger brother. Netflix “Books Are Leading the Charge” With the film coming amid a time when romance adaptations are continuing to make their way onscreen, the creative team says love stories are a “force to be reckoned with.” ROSENBAUM: The largely female audience reading the books is strong and vocal, so they’re guiding the studios toward what they like and what to make. I think that’s so democratic. When I started in this industry 25 years ago, that was not the case. It was really hard, first, to get directing gigs as a woman, and second, to get taken seriously with female content. SCHARBO: If you asked most people what they want more than anything in the world, the answer would be love. And books are leading the charge. It actually never went away in books. What happened is that movies took a pause from these stories. They got replaced by comic books, dark or action or genre, on the thinking that you need big spectacle to bring people to theaters. That’s not how movies originated, and it’s not how they are today. KEITH: Growing up in the ’90s, there were so many [love stories]. People our age who grew up with those movies were starved for them, and we want our kids to see love put on a pedestal. People were ready to see characters who weren’t in latex or didn’t have a superpower find each other. CARDILLO: The world feels a little dark and isolating for a lot of people right now. There’s something about reading about connection and love, and watching it on screen, that gives people a feeling of connectedness, hope and escape from what they’re dealing with. CENTER: Love stories are being treated more like a force to be reckoned with these days, which I love. Broadly speaking, it’s the most eye-rolled-at genre. For years I’ve been asking, why is people falling in love more ridiculous than zombies? This happens every day. Why do we believe in zombies but not humans? The fact that people are watching movies like this and reading books like this and standing up for love in this new way allows more stories like this to be told. It feels a little bit like a movement. *** Guarding Stars releases on Netflix on Nov. 18. THR

title: The Underdog Story Behind the Underdog Story
full_text: × Skip to main content Cover Story Alix Earle Bares All: How the TikToker Is Becoming Beauty’s Next Billion-Dollar Mogul close By Zach Goins Plus Icon Zach Goins View All November 18, 2026 9:44am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Sylvester Stallone as Rocky Balboa and Carl Weathers as Apollo Creed Image Courtesy of Amazon MGM Studios When Sylvester Stallone first walked into the offices of producers Irwin Winkler and Robert Chartoff , he was another struggling actor looking for his big break. The producers weren’t casting anything at the time, but as Stallone prepared to leave, he mentioned that he was also a writer. Intrigued, they invited him to send over a screenplay. Although Winkler and Chartoff passed on the initial script, they recognized Stallone’s potential and encouraged him to share whatever he wrote next. A week later, he returned with Rocky . Related Stories Movies 'Godzilla Minus Zero' Powers $31M in Historic Box Office Launch Against Subdued 'Cat in the Hat' Movies Golden Globes: 'I Play Rocky' Submitted as Comedy (Exclusive) “We thought it was really a great script,” Winkler recalled, nearly 50 years after the film’s release. “It was a story about somebody who has very little and believes in himself.” There was just one catch: Stallone insisted on playing the title character himself. “The studios were against it,” Winkler said. “They didn’t want to do the movie in general, and they certainly didn’t want to do it with him. But we persevered, just like he does in the movie.” Inspired in part by the real-life heavyweight bout between Muhammad Ali and underdog Chuck Wepner, the film’s central message was simple: Winning wasn’t necessarily about defeating your opponent, but proving you belonged in the ring in the first place. Sylvester Stallone as Rocky Balboa Image Courtesy of Amazon MGM Studios Working with an approximately $1 million budget, Winkler and Chartoff personally guaranteed the production’s costs, ultimately covering roughly $25,000 in overages themselves. The limited budget also forced the filmmakers to get creative. Take Rocky and Adrian’s romantic outing at the ice-skating rink. Initially intended to be a scene surrounded by other skaters, the filmmakers reimagined the scene with Rocky persuading a rink employee to let the couple skate alone after hours. “Because we couldn’t afford to hire extras, we did it with nobody, just because of the budget,” Winkler said. “I think it’s memorable because it’s just the two of them alone.” The result was a quietly intimate moment that captured the film’s emotional authenticity. Rather than disguising its modest resources, Rocky embraced them, grounding its characters in the everyday struggles of working-class Philadelphia . That authenticity would become one of the film’s defining qualities, helping transform a small independent production into an unlikely Hollywood sensation. Talia Shire as Adrian Pennino and Sylvester Stallone as Rocky Balboa Image Courtesy of Amazon MGM Studios For Winkler, the gamble began paying off when Stallone’s performance and composer Bill Conti ’s triumphant score finally came together. “We saw the strength of his performance, and then Bill Conti’s music on top of it,” Winkler said. “We said, ‘Okay, this is gonna be something.’” Released in 1976, Rocky became a box-office phenomenon, won three Academy Awards , including Best Picture, and launched a franchise that has endured for half a century. For filmmaker Peter Farrelly , the impact was immediate. “I just remember being blown away,” recalled Farrelly, who said he was about 18 years old the first time he saw Rocky in theaters. “I remember coming out of the theater and being like, ‘Woo!’ And I didn’t know what I was wooing about. I was inspired, but to do what, I didn’t know.” Sylvester Stallone as Rocky Balboa alongside Burgess Meredith as trainer Mickey Goldmill Image Courtesy of Amazon MGM Studios Farrelly likened the experience to watching his favorite team win a championship. He immediately began encouraging his friends to see the film, unaware that nearly five decades later, he would direct a movie about Rocky ’s creation. “Stallone’s story and Rocky’s story are identical, almost,” Farrelly said. That parallel became the foundation of I Play Rocky , Farrelly’s new film chronicling Stallone’s fight to bring his screenplay to the screen. For screenwriter Peter Gamble , the project was deeply personal. After spending years ghostwriting and contributing creatively to successful productions outside of the spotlight, Gamble began searching for an opportunity to establish himself as a writer in his own right. “I had this really weird experience of having done things that were really big, and people loved it, but they didn’t know me,” Gamble said. “I was invisible. I felt unseen.” When his manager suggested exploring Stallone’s story as a potential biopic, Gamble immediately recognized something of himself in the struggling actor who refused to accept Hollywood’s limitations. Inspired by Stallone’s famously rapid writing process, Gamble challenged himself to complete his own screenplay in approximately two weeks. But much like the original Rocky , getting the film made proved considerably more difficult than writing it. The project spent years in development as its producers struggled to secure financing, with the delays ultimately bringing the film’s release into alignment with Rocky ’s 50th anniversary. For Gamble, the connection between the two films extends beyond their unlikely journeys to the screen. At their core, both are stories about the universal desire to be recognized for what you have to offer. “Everyone has a moment where you go, ‘I feel like I got something in my heart and my soul that I can offer the universe if only someone would see it,’” Gamble said. Fifty years later, Rocky remains a reminder that sometimes going the distance is a victory in itself. THR

title: Up-and-Coming Filmmakers Talk About Their Craft, Challenges, Inspirations and More at Adobe TV & Film Fund Screening
full_text: Nov 18, 2026 9:30am PT Up-and-Coming Filmmakers Talk About Their Craft, Challenges, Inspirations and More at Adobe TV & Film Fund Screening By Todd Spangler Plus Icon Todd Spangler NY Digital Editor xpangler Latest Elon Musk Has Invested in Skydance, David Ellison Confirms: ‘To Have Him as a Shareholder Is an Honor’ 41 minutes ago Disney+ and Hulu App Merger Slated to Be Complete in December 1 day ago Disney Quarterly Revenue Rises 16% and Profit Doubles; Company Forecasts $3 Billion in Annual Cost Savings by 2029 Including Through Layoffs 1 day ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Pursuing a career as a filmmaker isn’t for the faint of heart. This week, three young creators who have been supported by the Adobe TV & Film Fund — Leo Aguirre, Michael Lei and Mel Mah — presented their short films at a special screening in Miami Beach hosted by Adobe and spoke about their work and what’s next. Variety moderated the conversation with the filmmakers in partnership with Adobe. The screening took place Nov. 10 at the Fillmore Miami Beach historic Art Deco theater, held during this year’s Adobe MAX 2026 creativity conference. Related Stories Skydance Reorgs TV and Streaming Distribution Leadership Team Post-Merger, Eight Execs to Exit James Gunn Says 'No One From Skydance' Has Seen 'Superman' Sequel 'Man of Tomorrow' as Rumors Fly After His DC Studios Exit Aguirre, a writer, director and visual artist raised on the U.S.-Mexico border, said his main advice to aspiring filmmakers is to “really believe in yourself.” “No one’s going to want to make your movie more than you,” he said. “Tell people to get on the train or get out of the way. And I think that’s the approach you have to have for your movie.” Mah, a writer, director, and producer from Toronto, said it’s important for filmmakers to “remember that art is created from the heart. Your mind is there to help, but it’s an emotional medium. And movies, the best ones, no matter what, they’re meant to move people.” She added that in addition to doing work on your scripts every day, you should “do things outside of film” to explore other passions and hobbies. “That’s what actually makes you a great filmmaker, because we’re telling stories about real life and you’ve got to go out there and live it in order to be to be able to tell those stories,” Mah said. Lei, an award-winning Chinese-born filmmaker, emphasized that it’s a difficult line of work. “It’s a really hard thing that to try to do film and it’s probably the most expensive art form, or one of the most expensive art forms, just because the amount of resources it takes to bring a crew and cast together and to do it convincingly,” he said. “You have to really, really love it and you have to want it for the right reasons,” Lei said. “It’s not a medium to get wealthy in. It’s not a medium to get famous.” Lei’s short that screened at the Adobe event was “The Rift,” a sci-fi-inflected story about a young man suspected of a mysterious affliction that makes him perceive the world in daylight while everyone, including his own father, sees darkness. Lei said it was the first public screening of “The Rift” — and he said it was gratifying to hear the response of a live audience. “I don’t know how to say this in other words, but it’s like, I will carry this on a hard day, you know? Like, I will remember this moment a few months from now where the writing is not coming or I get a rejection, but I’ll remember this moment and go, ‘You know, that’s what it’s worth it. This is what it’s for, exactly.'” Lei said “The Rift” will hopefully be a gateway for the story to become a feature-length film. “It’s a script that I’ve been carrying for the better part of the 2020s. And to have the opportunity through Adobe to actually go and film this proof of concept taught us so much,” he said. Aguirre’s short film “Isme” is about a tempestuous NYC teenager who steals a necklace from a woman on her deathbed — and “develops an obsession that leads her down a spiritually perilous path,” per the logline. “It’s a film about what we hold in this life and then what we hold in the next,” Aguirre said. “We all grew up with this idea of who we need to be. And then there’s artifice. And sometimes we feel completed by something that’s material.” Aguirre’s script for his debut feature, “Verano,” was selected for the 2025 Sundance Screenwriters & Directors Lab and is a recipient of the 2025-2026 Academy Nicholl Fellowship. “Verano,” which was supported by Adobe, was shot over the summer and Aguirre is hoping to premiere the film in the spring of 2027. “It was hard to get money. It was hard to get people to commit to helping us out,” said Aguirre. “But it was it was a very beautiful experience in so many ways.” Making “Isme” helped prepare him to embark on the feature film because he learned “how can we scale down and try to make the most of what we have.” Mah, who is a 2024 Women in Film directing fellow and founder of Decorum Pictures, also saw her short film “And That’s The Way The Cookie Crumbles” debut at the Adobe screening. The synopsis: A yoga influencer spirals into an existential crisis when a fortune cookie predicts her imminent death, and she begins to expose the hypocrisy of the mindfulness empire she’s built around a life she doesn’t actually live. “There’s so many things up there that I would have done differently, but there are so many things that also fell into place beautifully, too,” Mah said about her short film. “And I think that’s part of the beauty of filmmaking is we actually don’t have as much control as we think.” The story was somewhat autobiographical (Mah is herself a yoga and mindfulness teacher), but she said actress Dia Frampton, who plays the main character, “surprised me by bringing so much more of her spin on it. And I think because I’m so close to the character, I had imagined it maybe more in the way that I would be in that situation. But pleasantly surprised at how the performance was different.” Mah is currently developing her debut feature film “This Way to Home,” a road-trip dramedy starring Ken Jeong, with filming scheduled for spring 2027. “This Way to Home” was selected for Gold House’s Gold Pitch program at the Toronto International Film Festival and has secured CAN$1 million in production financing from Telefilm Canada. Each of the filmmakers were encouraged by the boom at the theatrical box office in 2026 , the best year for the industry since COVID. “I am a hopeless optimist, and I really think that we’re always going to be going to the theaters,” Mah said. “I don’t think anything’s going to replace that. And I do think there’s something in us that craves being in a room, quiet, seated all together and getting to experience the same emotions.” The trio also recounted how they realized they wanted to become filmmakers. Said Mah, “I’ve always been a storyteller, but maybe in a different way. My first passion was dance. I was a professional dancer for a long time, and that’s what took me from Toronto to Los Angeles originally. So from a young age, I started learning how to tell stories non-verbally and with my body. And then it was actually once I was living in Los Angeles that I started making my own dance films. And that’s when I realized that I wanted to step into filmmaking.” She added that her father “raised me on really great films. He taught me how to edit with Adobe.” “When I discovered filmmaking, it felt like something I could actually share with my parents — a passion that I could pursue that I knew they’d really be behind,” Mah said. Lei said that his own father similarly introduced him to film when the family emigrated to the U.S. “That’s that’s how we learned about culture. That’s how we learned the language. He was a huge Tom Cruise fan,” he said with a laugh. “We just grew up on, like, ‘Top Gun,’ ‘Days of Thunder,’ all that stuff. And we watched ‘The Godfather’ every Christmas because [my father] thought it was a Christmas movie, because there’s that one scene that takes place at Christmas.” But the big moment for Lei was when he was living in New York during 9/11 and watching the first Oscars that took place afterward in March 2002. “And there was a really beautiful monologue at the beginning of that, which was serendipitously given by Tom Cruise , and he talked about the magic of movies and storytelling, and it was such a sensitive time for us as a community in New York,” he said. “And I just remember thinking, movies had been such a profound thing for me, growing up. And it was really meaningful. And I guess you could say Tom Cruise told me to make movies that day, but that was probably like the flashbulb moment for me.” Aguirre said he grew up in El Paso and his grandparents lived just across the border in Mexico. “I’d spend the summers there watching anything that my grandpa was watching… like these golden age Mexican films,” he said. While Aguirre originally wanted to be an actor, “my parents were like, ‘That’s a terrible idea.’ And then one summer I did this [theater] workshop and I thought, ‘I don’t want to act on the stage anymore. I want to try to do it for the screen.’ And then I liked being behind the camera a lot more. And that was a kind of natural progression.” Rosalía, Hilary Duff, and Slayyyter to Be Honored at Variety’s Hitmakers Event Olivia Rodrigo, Katseye and Sienna Spiro to Be Honored at Variety’s 10th Annual Hitmakers Event Raye Named Variety’s 2026 Hitmaker of the Year Loading comments...

title: Cold War Thriller ‘Goldsboro’ Moves Forward With Erik Jendresen & Howard A. Rodman Scripting For Permut Presentations, AETH Entertainment
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Vin Diesel To Star In Action Pic 'Burial Hill'; Amazon Closing Big Deal Read the full story By Matt Grobar Matt Grobar Senior Film Reporter More Stories By Matt New ‘Friday The 13th’ Movie Unveils Cast, Title & Release Date Darian Lanzetta Out At Mattel Studios Comedians Leah Rudick & Jessica Michelle Singleton Launch ‘People Pleasers’ Podcast With PodcastOne View All November 18, 2026 9:25am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Erik Jendresen, Howard A. Rodman Getty/AMPAS EXCLUSIVE: In 2021, we announced development on a feature adaptation of Joel Dobson ‘s nonfiction book The Goldsboro Broken Arrow . Five years later, the project has gained new momentum, as Erik Jendresen ( Band of Brothers ) and Howard A. Rodman ( Savage Grace ) have come aboard to pen the period thriller for Hacksaw Ridge producer David Permut ‘s Permut Presentations and AETH Entertainment . Set at the height of the Cold War, Goldsboro tells the extraordinary true story of the January 1961 crash of a U.S. Air Force B-52 near Goldsboro, North Carolina. The aircraft was carrying two thermonuclear weapons when it broke apart in midair, sending the bombs toward the farmland below and bringing the United States to the brink of nuclear catastrophe. The film will explore the experiences of the Goldsboro townsfolk, the military personnel confronting the crisis, and the human decisions made in the shadow of a catastrophe that could have changed the course of history. Related Stories News How Indie Comedy 'The Invite' Crashed The Summer Blockbuster Party; Is The Next Stop Broadway? News 'Little Death' Helmer Jack Begert Teams With David Permut & Undisputed Pictures For Biopic On LSD-Fueled No-Hitting MLB Pitcher Dock Ellis Dobson, a former U.S. Air Force officer who served with Strategic Air Command during the 1960s, spent years researching the Goldsboro incident and interviewing many of the people directly involved. His book provides a detailed account of the doomed B-52 mission, its crew, the recovery operation, and the circumstances and war games surrounding one of the most extraordinary nuclear incidents of the Cold War. Watch on Deadline The story’s themes carry new weight today, with the advent of AI, a technology Bill Gates has warned “makes nuclear weapons look like nothing,” posing the threat of great disruption. Coming off a pair of lauded 2026 releases — the A24 chamber drama The Invite and Apple disability rights drama Being Heumann — Permut told Deadline, “Some true stories almost defy belief, and GOLDSBORO is one of them.” He’s set to produce alongside Eric Woods and Carla Woods for AETH Entertainment, Michael Alfieri and Sterling Macer, Jr. Permut Presentations’ Head of Development, Alex Astrachan, will serve as executive producer. Eric Woods of AETH said, “We knew the key to telling this story would be finding the humanity within an event of such enormous historical significance. Erik Jendresen and Howard Rodman are extraordinary storytellers with a remarkable ability to bring complex, character-driven stories to life. They are the ideal team to explore the lives of the people caught in the middle of this extraordinary event.” No stranger to war stories, Jendresen served as lead writer and supervising producer of HBO’s acclaimed WWII miniseries Band of Brothers , sharing in its Emmy win for Outstanding Miniseries and receiving an Emmy nomination for writing. His recent feature work includes co-writing Mission: Impossible – Dead Reckoning and Mission: Impossible — The Final Reckoning with Christopher McQuarrie. Rodman is a screenwriter, novelist and educator whose credits include Savage Grace , starring Julianne Moore and Eddie Redmayne; August ; and Joe Gould’s Secret . His screenplay for Savage Grace received an Independent Spirit Award nomination. A former chair of USC’s screenwriting program and an Artistic Director of the Sundance Screenwriting Labs, he’s a past President of the Writers Guild of America West and is currently Vice President of AMPAS. Permut’s The Invite grossed over $62M worldwide — no small feat for an indie drama in the 2020s — and was just nominated for four Gotham Awards, including Best Picture. His other credits range from Face/Off to the lauded WWII medic drama Hacksaw Ridge , which received two Academy Awards and earned him a Best Picture nomination. His latest film Being Heumann , directed by CODA Oscar winner Sian Heder, opened worldwide on November 6. AETH Entertainment’s Eric and Carla Woods have produced over 150 films and series, with credits including Looking Through Water starring Michael Douglas, Christmas with the Campbells , Spread , and Incarcerated . As the bipartisan incentive initiative appears to be stalling in the lame duck Congress, Ellison cited stats from not just Canada, the UK and Australia on the usefulness of tax credits to attracting production and creating jobs, but also noted the return on investment previous solid red Texas has seen in recent years. title: Nicolas Cage on His Approach to Playing John Madden in New Biopic: “I’m Not an Impressionist”
full_text: × Skip to main content Cover Story Alix Earle Bares All: How the TikToker Is Becoming Beauty’s Next Billion-Dollar Mogul close By Kirsten Chuba Plus Icon Kirsten Chuba Events Editor kirstenchuba Follow Sign Up View All November 18, 2026 9:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Nicolas Cage and wife Riko Shibata attend the world premiere of Amazon MGM Studios' "Madden" at The Culver Theater on Nov. 4. Axelle/Bauer-Griffin/FilmMagic John Madden may be one of the most notable figures in sports history, but he was unknown to Nicolas Cage before the actor portrayed him in new movie Madden . “He was not on my radar. I was growing up watching black-and-white Orson Welles movies and Fellini movies and Bruce Lee. I wasn’t interested in team sports whatsoever,” Cage, a member of the cinema-centric Coppola family, explains. That didn’t stop David O. Russell from casting him in the film , which follows Madden’s journey from a Super Bowl-winning coach to creating the Madden NFL video game and becoming a beloved commentator. Intertwined in that story is Raiders owner Al Davis (played by Christian Bale ), who was Madden’s best friend on and off the field; Russell originally came to Cage to play Davis, which he rejected. Related Stories Movies 'Madden' Review: Nicolas Cage and Christian Bale Go for Broke in a Cartoonish Biopic From David O. Russell That's Strictly for Football Fanatics Movies John Mulaney Teases His 'Get Smart' Reboot: "My Favorite Type of Person to Play" When the director came back with the idea that he play Madden instead, “because I’m someone that likes to stay out of his comfort zone and take a risk, I said yes, because that would be a transformation,” Cage says. “It would be something where I might learn a few things, taking on this character who is really nothing like me.” “That’s what acting’s about. I’m not an impressionist, I’m not [Madden impersonator] Frank Caliendo,” he continues. “I lean more towards being a surrealist, meaning I like to get a concept of a personality and then dig deep and see what I can locate emotionally with my imagination and my psyche and filter it through the cadence and the appearance, within reason, of John Madden. I’m trying to give you an evocation, more or less, or an interpretation.” That’s also how Cage approached Madden’s famous voice, saying, “I listened to his cadence, I located what I thought would be an interpretation within the realms of what was anatomically possible. I’m not going to let AI touch my voice or my appearance. I try to give you something which is an interpretation.” The film — with a starry supporting cast that includes Kathryn Hahn, Sienna Miller, John Mulaney and Shane Gillis — also brings together two actors who famously go deep into their roles, in Cage and Bale. Cage says the two are “very different kinds of actors” who had a “great time riffing off of each other,” while Bale notes that “there’s no competition in that at all” in how they face-off on screen. “I’ve admired Nic for many, many years, going all the way back to Rumble Fish , which is absolutely one of my favorite movies ever,” Bale says. “He’s not only a fascinating actor but a very interesting man himself. He’s lived a hell of a life, just like Al Davis, just like John Madden, just like David O. Russell. There were some real characters involved in creating this film.” This marks the fourth collaboration between Russell and Bale, following The Fighter , American Hustle and Amsterdam . The star said that when he and the director “approach a film, we always think this might just be the last one we ever get to make. That’s the right attitude to have with movies, and in the state of movies right now, it might very well be the truth. But it’s a wonderful attitude to have,” commending the filmmaker for the way “he loves actors so much.” Madden is now streaming on Prime Video. THR

title: Celebrity Beauty Brands (Even Kim’s) Are Failing. Here Are the New Rules
full_text: × Skip to main content Cover Story Alix Earle Bares All: How the TikToker Is Becoming Beauty’s Next Billion-Dollar Mogul close G wen Stefani’s GXVE Beauty is gone. So are Scarlett Johansson ‘s skin care line The Outset and Serena Williams’ Wyn Beauty cosmetics. Even Kim Kardashian ‘s KKW Beauty and SKKN by Kim have been retired. Blake Lively ‘s Blake Brown Beauty hair care is struggling, and Jennifer Lopez ‘s JLO Beauty has quietly exited Sephora. Yes, the celebrity beauty business is crowded and unforgiving, but that still hasn’t stopped Cardi B and Jennifer Lawrence from joining the fray. Cardi B, for one, remains undeterred. “People are always going to have something to say, but I didn’t create Grow-Good just to put my name on a bottle. Hair care has always been personal to me. I’ve been sharing my hair routines, my homemade treatments and my hair journey with my fans for years, way before I ever thought about launching a brand.” Related Stories THR Digital Cover Hudson Williams and His Hairstylist Aika Flores Really Are That Close THR Cover Story Alix Earle Bares All: How the TikToker Is Becoming Beauty's Next Billion-Dollar Mogul Blake Lively Blake Brown Beauty With a stake in a brand worth potentially far more than a movie deal as production slates threaten to continue shrinking, it’s easy to understand why Hollywood keeps lining up. The success stories are seductive: Rihanna ‘s Fenty Beauty helped make her a billionaire, Selena Gomez ‘s Rare Beauty has been valued at $2.7 billion, and Hailey Bieber’s Rhode sold to e.l.f. Beauty in a deal worth up to $1 billion. Selena Gomez’s Rare Beauty, valued at $2.7 billion, is an increasingly rare example of wild success in a crowded market. But fame doesn’t always bring fortune — or an easy ride. In October, Lawrence launched Mes (pronounced “mess”) with Arcaea CEO Jasmina Aganovic, generating plenty of buzz and a fair amount of backlash over what online critics complained was another example of celebrity overreach. The partnership reportedly began after Lawrence watched Aganovic deliver a TED Talk about the future of cosmetics. Aganovic leads Arcaea, a biotech company developing sustainable, high-performance cosmetic ingredients that has counted Chanel among its investors, and she brings serious beauty credentials, having previously worked at Living Proof and led skin-microbiome brand Mother Dirt. Mes embraces an “unbothered beauty” philosophy, with the enticing promise of achieving great hair without putting in lots of time or effort. It also plays into Lawrence’s public persona as the rare A-lister with genuinely self-deprecating, what-you-see-is-what-you-get candor. The actress introduced the line, which includes a hair mask, serum and volume mist, on Instagram as one for “nice people who don’t leave mean comments.” It was almost as if she knew what was coming. (Per her reps, Lawrence was not available to comment for this report.) After years away from social media, Lawrence made her debut Sept. 9, just weeks before the launch, and the timing didn’t go unnoticed. Some commenters smelled a calculated sales pitch. Others questioned the fit, noting she’s never been especially known for her hair. To skeptics and Reddit users, it looked like one more celebrity chasing a Rhode-sized payday. Lawrence, for her part, said the line grew out of years in the glam chair, when she would wash her hair only once a week. “At this point in the life cycle of celebrity brands, the initial reaction is always going be the eye roll,” says Aliza Licht, marketing veteran and author of On Brand . “We all have the playbook now and everybody knows what’s behind the curtain.” Often, that’s a licensing deal, a manufacturer, a hefty marketing budget and a carefully crafted backstory, with the star’s name as the cherry on top. “Consumers are good at recognizing an engineered marketing narrative dressed up as a personal passion project.” Kim Kardashian SKKN Stefanie Keenan/Getty Images Beauty publicist Marie-Laure Fournier, founder of Fournier PR + Consulting, believes the criticism around Mes is still manageable. “A candid, even humorous video with Aganovic, whether with a magazine or on social media, could go a long way toward humanizing the launch and addressing the skepticism head on,” she says. “The public wants to see that you’re listening, learning and willing to adapt.” Despite some of the backlash, the early industry read on Mes is cautiously optimistic. Lawrence’s working with Aganovic is “a good move, to partner with a brand like Arcaea that is well established in the beauty industry,” says Clare Hennigan, principal analyst for beauty and consumer goods at global research firm Mintel. Hennigan also sees promise in the products, particularly a gel hair mask that can be applied to dry hair and doubles as a styler. No need to wait for wash day. “They are solving a pain point of convenience, a key motivator for purchases,” she says. “Anything that makes life a little easier is something shoppers will pay more for.” Kate Hudson would applaud this solution-oriented approach for the consumer. The celebrity entrepreneur co-founded Fabletics in 2013, remains a shareholder and watched the activewear company reportedly surpass $1 billion in revenue in 2025. “You can have the most beautiful vision in the world, but once you put something out there, you have to pay attention to what they need, what they love and what they don’t,” she says. Jennifer Lawrence’s Mes hair care line was met with skepticism. Delivering effective products is one thing; fostering a genuine connection with the consumer is another. Cardi B out of the gate demonstrated a keen understanding of the latter with marketing Grow-Good. Her grassroots strategy focuses on neighborhood beauty supply stores, including shops in her native Bronx. The hair care line, following three years of development, debuted in April and reportedly sold out in less than 35 minutes. “Listen, I know my people because I am my people!” she says. “I grew up going to beauty supply stores. Those stores have always been part of our community, and I wanted Grow-Good to be there too. For me, it was about making sure the products were accessible to the people I created them for.” Lisa Motzko Hamilton, former vp of merchandising at Ulta Beauty and co-founder of Breakthru Beauty consultancy, says brands perform best when the entertainer is “showing up, engaging with their community and sharing a part of themselves beyond their celebrity status.” The Business of Fashion reports a promising 40 percent return-customer rate for Grow-Good. Even more critically, the celebrity and the product need to make sense together. Lady Gaga’s Haus Labs cosmetics draw on her reputation for artistry and creative expression, while Selena Gomez built Rare Beauty around supporting mental health for young people, a cause she has publicly owned as a personal issue, with 1 percent of sales going to Rare Impact Fund. Hennigan cites Jennifer Aniston ‘s LolaVie as a brand that gets it very right. Aniston’s hairstyles have been a cultural fixture for decades, making hair care a natural fit. She spent several years developing the line before launching in 2021 and has since expanded to Ulta and Credo. “LolaVie is very personal to me. My relationship with my hair, the products I’ve tried over the years and the challenges I’ve experienced are what inspired the brand in the first place,” says Aniston. “I didn’t want to simply put my name on something; I wanted to be part of building something that I truly believed in.” Jennifer Aniston’s LolaVie hair care line has staying power, partially because she keeps herself connected to consumers: “We’ve made changes to product based on feedback.” The Morning Show star also makes a point of keeping a conversation going with customers. “I love hearing how other people incorporate the products into their routines and about the results they’re seeing. We’ve made changes to product in the past based on consumer feedback,” she says. (She’s also extended LolaVie into pet shampoo: “My dogs are such a big part of my family, and I wanted to bring the same thoughtfulness and attention to detail that goes into our human hair care.” All profits benefit The Clydeo Fund, which supports animal rescue and rehabilitation.) Author Licht points to Kardashian as someone who has spent years cultivating “a parasocial bond with followers, so a new brand lands with people she already knows, even the haters.” Stars who suddenly surface hawking new products are a harder sell. “It’s odd when we hear from celebrities out of the blue,” she says. “We don’t have social relationships with them, they’re movie stars.” Licht adds that Lawrence, who had no public social media presence until weeks before the launch, “seemed to come out of thin air,” she says. “We are missing a bit of evidence there.” Scarlett Johansson The Outset Ilya S. Savenok/Getty Images Johansson’s The Outset offers another cautionary tale. “We didn’t have historical commentary from Scarlett around skin care,” says Licht. “The consumer needs to find a germ of a connection between the celebrity and the brand.” Hennigan sees another issue: “The problem was proof. The efficacy and science may not have been as visible to shoppers.” Lopez faced a different kind of disconnect with potential consumers. A merchandising executive at a beauty retailer, speaking on condition of anonymity, questions JLO Beauty’s origin story. “Jennifer hung the age-defying ‘JLo Glow’ on a family olive oil secret, but doubters online, including a chorus of dermatologists, weren’t convinced it was the whole story with JLO Beauty,” creating an issue with consumer trust. Jennifer Lopez JLO Beauty AaronP/Bauer-Griffin/GC Images/Getty Images Blake Lively’s Blake Brown Beauty hair care line launched to considerable fanfare at Target, only to face a more complicated reality as the actress became embroiled in the fallout surrounding It Ends With Us and her legal battle with Justin Baldoni. Lively went quiet on social media, and sales have reportedly dropped sharply. “The war with Justin was likely a huge detriment to sales,” says Licht. Distribution matters, too. Lady Gaga’s Haus Labs initially launched exclusively on Amazon, a challenging fit for color cosmetics, where shoppers want to try on shades before buying. Its move to Sephora introduced the brand to a broader beauty audience. Then comes the most important question of all: Does the world really need another beauty line? Gwen Stefani GXVE Beauty Fenty Beauty answered that question nearly a decade ago with an expansive and inclusive shade range that addressed a glaring gap in the cosmetics market. Rhode found its opening with accessible pricing on ingredients that had become associated with more expensive skin care. “Peptides were drawing a lot of attention, with many brands charging a premium for them, while Bieber offered high-performing peptide products at a more affordable price,” notes Hennigan. For Mes, even in light of its messy debut, Hennigan sees an opportunity to shift the conversation toward time-saving efficiency with education: “Help consumers understand how these products fit into their existing hair care routines. Since the hair mask comes with a learning curve, the brand needs to drive the how-to aspect home” with tutorials and partnerships with pro stylists who can demo the products, she advises. Ultimately, the biggest challenge of the enterprise may be the least glamorous part: remaining involved long after the cameras and launch parties. Hudson, who joined HealthyCell supplements as an investor and creative strategy partner in October, says patience is the X factor. “I’ve learned that building a business is a long game,” she says. “You have to love the process, not just the excitement of launching something.” Licht doesn’t mince words: “Most of the time celebrities are just not cut out for the daily grind required to build a brand, and that’s why a lot of these lines fail.” Additional reporting by Beth Landman. This story appeared in the Nov. 18 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.

title: David Ellison Says There Might Be “Some News Sharing In The Future” Between CBS And CNN
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Vin Diesel To Star In Action Pic 'Burial Hill'; Amazon Closing Big Deal Read the full story By Ted Johnson Ted Johnson Political Editor @tedstew More Stories By Ted Hakeem Jeffries Poised To Become Next House Speaker After Winning Overwhelming Support Of Democratic Caucus Democrats Boycott Senate Commerce Committee Vote To Advance Republican FCC Nominee Another Day, Another Outage: As CNN Reports On NSA Network Down, News Outlets Seize On Back-To-Back Incidents Of Cyber Chaos View All November 18, 2026 8:56am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Skydance CEO David Ellison Gilbert Flores/Variety Skydance CEO David Ellison said that the company is “incredibly happy” operating CNN and CBS News as they are, but suggested that there “might be some news sharing in the future.” Ellison’s comments, during The New York Times’ DealBook Summit, hint at a possible new arrangement for the two news giants, which have operated independently since Skydance closed its deal to purchase Warner Bros. Discovery last month. Andrew Ross Sorkin asked Ellison whether he sees “a point a year from now, two years from now, where these institutions merge.” Related Stories News Hakeem Jeffries Poised To Become Next House Speaker After Winning Overwhelming Support Of Democratic Caucus News Democrats Boycott Senate Commerce Committee Vote To Advance Republican FCC Nominee “Right now, we are incredibly happy operating them basically within the status quo,” Ellison said. “I think you also have … there might be some news sharing in the future. But right now we’re operating them as they are.” Watch on Deadline As the time of the deal close, CNN’s Mark Thompson has remained atop the news organization, while Bari Weiss has continued to serve as editor in chief of CBS News. But Skydance is under the gun to cut costs, and announced a companywide offering of buyouts. Ellison also addressed a topic he has previously discussed: Restoring trust in the news media. After citing polling showing low trust in news media overall, Ellison said, “I think it’s important when you are getting that feedback from the audience to make sure that you are working to rebuild trust every single day. I also think it’s really important to be truly basic truth-based, bipartisan, down the middle as you’re basically delivering news. And again, when you look at what our goal for for news is, and we’re we’re one year into this journey, is to make sure that we can rebuild trust back to at least where it was previously, if not even higher.” He added, “The thing that I am also very proud of is we have incredible journalists that are showing up every single day to accomplish that goal. That is our mission today. That is our mission tomorrow. That will be our mission five years from now. And fundamentally, we will not stop working until we earn that trust, and from an editorial standpoint, we believe in editorial independence. We don’t get involved basically in those decisions, but we trust the journalists will do their jobs incredibly well.” Ellison also confirmed that Elon Musk was a shareholder in Skydance, after reports that Musk had invested $1 billion. He declined to say whether the investment was the start of something bigger with Musk’s Starlink. “If there was an appropriate opportunity in the future, we would be thrilled to do so, but there is nothing we can comment on.” Asked by Sorkin whether Skydance would put Alex Gibney’s Musk documentary on HBO, Ellison noted that they have a deal with A24, the producer of the project, and “of course we’re going to honor the deal.” Pressed further by Sorkin on whether that meant that they would air the project, Ellison said, “We believe in independence. We don’t believe in censorship of any kind. And again, we have that deal with A24. Of course we’ll honor it.” Ellison also defended the company’s approach to winning federal approval for the Paramount -Warner Bros. Discovery merger. Sorkin cited Ellison’s meetings with Donald Trump and “making yourself look like you were closer to the president than it seems like you’re suggesting you are.” Ellison said, “Our goal was to close the Paramount transaction, close the Warner Brothers transaction. We accomplished our goal. We worked with regulators basically on both sides of the aisle, and and ultimately everybody came to the same conclusion.” He then noted that he had spoken to Hakeem Jeffries, poised to become the next House Speaker, “multiple times in the past,” as well as Chuck Schumer. Ellison responded, “So look, I have so much admiration and respect for Elon. I mean, I don’t know if you saw recently, but literally watching, you know, [SpaceX’s] Starship, it’s a marvel…. I mean, he is both the [Nikola] Tesla and [Thomas] Edison… He is, from my perspective, the greatest entrepreneur of our time, and he doesn’t invest in a lot of companies.” Ellison continued, “So to have his vote of confidence and to have him as a shareholder is an honor and a privilege. And if there was any opportunity to be able to collaborate with him in the future… [which] is the appropriate opportunity in the future, we’d be thrilled to do so. But there’s nothing [right now].” Sorkin asked Ellison whether he is still planning to put Alex Gibney’s documentary “Musk” — which prompted a legal threat from the tech titan against the filmmaker — on HBO. (“Musk” has been pegged to begin streaming on HBO Max in the first quarter of 2027.) Ellison responded, “Of course.” Ellison’s Paramount Skydance closed its $111 billion megamerger with Warner Bros. Discovery on Oct. 6 , with major backing from his father, Oracle billionaire Larry Ellison. The company, one of the biggest media and entertainment conglomerates in the industry, has around $80 billion in net debt and is expected to lay off thousands of employees as part of achieving $6 billion in annualized savings by 2029. The Ellison family — with the multibillion-dollar backing of Larry Ellison — holds the largest equity stake in Skydance. RedBird Capital Partners, led by managing partner Gerry Cardinale, invested $4 billion into Skydance , and philanthropist and investor Laurene Powell Jobs, founder and president of Emerson Collective, has invested $250 million . Equity investors in the Paramount-WBD merger also included the sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Abu Dhabi. The Ellisons and investment firm RedBird Capital Partners together are the sole holders of Paramount Class A common stock, including 100% of the combined company’s voting shares. title: Bellevue Productions Hires Literary Manager David Baggelaar
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Vin Diesel To Star In Action Pic 'Burial Hill'; Amazon Closing Big Deal Read the full story By Matt Grobar Matt Grobar Senior Film Reporter More Stories By Matt New ‘Friday The 13th’ Movie Unveils Cast, Title & Release Date Darian Lanzetta Out At Mattel Studios Comedians Leah Rudick & Jessica Michelle Singleton Launch ‘People Pleasers’ Podcast With PodcastOne View All November 18, 2026 8:45am Add us as a Google Preferred Source David Baggelaar Catie Laffoon EXCLUSIVE: Bellevue Productions , the literary management and production company led by President John Zaozirny, has announced the hiring of literary manager David Baggelaar , who joins following more than a decade at Benderspink and its successor company, Good Fear. Bringing with him a roster of film and television writers, directors and IP creators, Baggelaar will continue developing his existing clients while working to expand Bellevue’s roster across both film and television. Clients joining Baggelaar include Monisha Dadlani ( The Marigold Paradox ), Julian Terry ( Don’t Peek ), Michael Feldman & Debbie Jhoon ( A.P. Bio , Not Dead Yet ), Rohit Kumar ( 13 Reasons Why , Wheel of Time ), Min-Woo Park ( Grey’s Anatomy ), Brandi Nicole ( Your Honor , Ballard ), Woody Strassner ( FBI ), Amelia Sims ( S.W.A.T. ) and Barnett Brettler ( Black Mad Wheel ). Baggelaar’s production experience includes work on New Line’s We’re the Millers , Horrible Bosses 2 and Vacation , as well as Disney’s Mulan , and serving as an associate producer on A24’s Under the Silver Lake . He told us, “From my first conversations with the Bellevue team, I felt an immediate connection. Their client-first approach and genuine dedication to the craft of development are exactly what I was looking for, both for myself and for those I represent, and I couldn’t be more excited to build the next chapter of my career here.” Bellevue’s Zaozirny said, “David’s deep industry experience, keen eye for talent, and extensive background in production make him an incredibly exciting manager to work alongside and we’re lucky to have him at Bellevue. We can’t wait to see how he continues to develop the amazing clients he’s already working with and what bold new voices he’ll be signing now that he’s here.” Founded in 2015, Bellevue is known for its knack for breaking emerging writers. Clients have placed 72 scripts on the last 11 Black Lists, with No. 1 scripts in 2016, 2020, 2021 and 2025. The company’s upcoming production slate includes Paramount’s K-Pop: The Debut and Warner Bros.’ Shiver , both scheduled for theatrical release in 2027.
