title: Doha Film Festival
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Vin Diesel To Star In Action Pic 'Burial Hill', Amazon Closing Big Deal Read the full story By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Qatar’s Film Committee Head Hassan Al-Thawadi Teases 2nd Industry Days In Doha: “We Are moving From Vision To Execution” ‘Chronicles From The Siege’ Producers Pull Palestinian Berlinale Prizewinner From Marrakech Jean-Pierre & Luc Dardenne Set For European Film Academy Lifetime Achievement Award View All November 17, 2026 12:25am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Naomi Kawase, James Gray, Nandita Das; (inset) 'The Station' Getty Images Organizing a film festival is a challenge at the best of times, figuring out the logistics with the threat of war on the doorstep requires an extra layer of resilience. It is a quality Fatma Al Remaihi, CEO of the Doha Film Institute (DFI) and her team have had to muster in spades as they prepared for the second edition of the rebooted Doha Film Festival , setting in place logistics for a trio of different scenarios. “We knew that no matter what, we will have a festival… we were exploring differing scenarios, that it could be just for locals, that it could be for everyone, or that it could just be an online competition. We’ve planned for every eventuality,” Al Remaihi tells Deadline on the eve of the festival which is due to open on Thursday. She is speaking nine months after Israel and the U.S. launched a major military campaign against Iran’s Islamic Republic government at the end of February, which retaliated with missile and drone strikes on all its Gulf neighbors. The DFI was forced to move its popular annual Qumra project and talent incubator online in March, with the team applying lessons learned during the Covid-19 pandemic. While guests, including Gael García Bernal, Diego Luna and Alice Diop, could not make it to Qatar , Al Remaihi says the event still fulfilled its mission. “The filmmakers and the projects didn’t miss this edition. It was fantastic to be able to be there for them. Even though a lot of our staff here were suffering with scary times, they’re still pulled through and made it happen for the filmmakers.” The situation has calmed down since April and Qatar has been heavily involved in negotiations to deescalate the conflict, with its diplomats regularly traveling to the Iranian capital Tehran as part of international efforts to broker a peace deal. Al Remaihi is confident that the festival, running from November 19 to 27, will unfold at full capacity, alongside other events set to take place in Doha in the period including the Fashion Trust Arabia Awards on November 28 and the Formula 1 Grand Prix from November 27 to 28. “We’re so happy that we are a few days away from the festival, and excited now to open and experience it with everybody, and it’s not smaller, we have more films and more guests,” she says. The festival expands on the DFI’s long-running family-focused festival of Ajyal which ran for more than a decade during the same period, with Media City Qatar and the territory’s Film Committee coming on board as new partners as part of their mission to build the country’s media and entertainment sector. “I don’t like to call it a second edition as I don’t see it as a new festival. It’s a continuation of what we do,” notes Al Remaihi, while acknowledging that the repositioning gave the festival fresh impetus last year. The first edition of the reboot set the tone for a festival focused on cinema and rather than big name stars. “The guests that we invite are from the program. That’s what is important for us. They have a role in the program and something to give in the festival. It’s never been about big names and stars for us,” says Al Remaihi. She points nonetheless to the presence of Japanese director Naomi Kawase as jury president for the main International Competition; James Gray , for a gala screening of Paper Tiger , and Oscar-winning documentarian Gianfranco Rosi ,who is also on the jury alongside rising actor Adam Bessa, Tunisian producer Dora Bouchoucha and Palestinian director Kamal Aljafari. Related Stories News Festival In Focus: Qatar Ramps Up International Film & TV Ambitions As Local Talent Shines News Festival In Focus: Marrakech's Atlas Workshops Nurtures Bespoke Approach As Project Incubator Goes From Strength-To-Strength Indian filmmaker and actor Nandita Das ( Manto , Zwigato ) and regional star, the Syrian actor Taim Hassan ( Al Hayba , Mawlana ), will also be in attendance to receive the festival’s Creative Excellence Award. “We have big names. Maybe for the public eyes, it’s different. But for people who work in the industry and who value filmmaking and the craft itself, they know these names and they’re very excited to have them in Doha. In that sense, I’m very happy with the caliber of the guests who are coming to the festival,” she explains. Watch on Deadline The Station Screen Project, Georges Films DFI-backed Yemen-set drama The Station by Sara Ishaq – set against the backdrop of woman-only petrol stations in the war-torn country – opens this edition. “We confirmed The Station for the opening months ago. It’s very rare to have an opening film confirmed from that early, but we saw in this film everything that embodies the festival and the spirit of the festival,” says Al Remaihi. “It’s a simple story that sheds light on a very complicated background, and we thought it was very brave to make a film like this. We don’t see a lot coming out of Yemen. Yes, it had its premiere in Cannes, but we wanted to give it center stage in the festival.” The Station is among 15 films playing in the International Competition at the heart of the festival, competing for close to $200,000 in combined prize money. It features a raft of titles which have garnered acclaim on the festival circuit over the past year including Cameroonian director Auguste Bernard Kouemo’s House of the Wind , which won Venice’s Lion of the Future for a Debut Film when it premiered there in its Orizzonti sidebar in September. Further contenders include Moroccan director Tala Hadid’s Bardi , which played at the New York Film Festival, and Thai filmmaker Sompot Chidgasornpongse’s 9 Temples to Heaven , which premiered in Cannes Directors’ Fortnight and is Thailand’s submission to the 99th Academy Awards. Other Oscar hopefuls in the lineup include the Philippines’ entry Filipiñana by Rafael Manuel and Chilean director Manuela Martelli’s The Meltdown . There are four films by Palestinian filmmakers including Rabab Khamis’ documentary Sama , about a ten-year-old girl who collects plastic and cardboard in Deir al-Balah in Gaza to sell as fuel and help sustain her family, which world premieres It is joined by Hosam Abu Dan’s Gaza-shot drama Thirteen in Gaza , about a 13-year-old living with her father in a Gaza displacement camp, which won the NETPAC Award in Toronto; Muayad Alayan’s Venice–selected Conversation with the Sea , about a Palestinian man caught in the crosshairs of Israeli bureaucracy, and Mohanad Yaqubi’s Revolutionaries Never Die , revolving around 113 reels of films preserved by Lebanese filmmaker Jocelyne Saab. The final contenders are Asmahan Bkerat’s Concrete Land, Hugo Salvaterra’s My Semba, Zou Jing Cannes Critics’ Week Fipresci-winner A Girl Unknown , Alessandra Sanguinetti’s The Illusion of an Everlasting Summer and Alexander Murphy’s Tin Castle . Eleven of the films have received the support of the DFI’s grantee programs, with Al Remaihi explaining it is at the heart of an interconnected process developed over the institute’s 16-year existence. “It just shows that we don’t do anything on a singular basis. Everything we do is connected. We have an ecosystem that we built a long time ago, and we’ve seen the benefits of having something like this,” she says. “A lot of the films in our competition are grantees because it speaks to the type of funding that we do, choices that we make, the people that we work with, and we love to celebrate all of this during the festival with all of that community. It’s a great moment for us also to have all of that come together.” Outside of the competition, there will be gala screening for Paper Tige r, Rami Kodeih’s DFI-backed Beirut-set heist thriller Furies, Maiken Baird’s Toronto-selected Edward Said: Between Worlds and Bruno Dumont’s Red Rocks . Fatma Al Remaihi on the red carpet at the 2025 Doha Film Festival Getty Images There will also be Special Screenings for Abderrahmane Sissako’s Artou , Daniele Rugo’s Life Support , following international doctors working alongside local medical staff in Gaza in 2023; Ginevra Elkann drama The Roses of Marrakech and Ali El Arabi’s 52 Blue . Another key strand is the Made In Qatar sidebar. This has traditionally showcased short films but makes history this year as it premieres f our locally produced features , spanning Jodari Meno by Jamal Al Khanji, A Very Ordinary Life by Mohamed Deniz, First to Fly by Rodrigo Vazquez Salessi and When the News Breaks You by Hamad Al Hajri. “It’s a testament to all of the work that we’ve been doing over the years and how the industry has developed in Qatar. We’ve been doing this for a long time, but now its not just the Doha Film Institute. We the Film Committee, Media City Qatar, and Katara Studios, all the film production houses,” she says. “You feel that there is a huge movement and a huge shift in the industry here.” A new addition is the Cinema Alkhaleej sidebar showcasing cinema from across the Gulf region, with highlights including the world premiere of horror feature Soulala by Saudi director and actor Hisham Fqih as well as the Qatar premiere of Ahd Kamel’s My Driver and I , which originally premiered at Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea International Film Festival in 2024. “We wanted to bring the Khaleeji (Gulf) industry together and have them more involved in the festival, not just as guests but also as participating guests. A lot of these films were not available here, so they are still fresh for our audiences. I loved watching all these films as we programmed the section and I’m excited to share them with the audience here.” ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ Turns Chaos & Crime Into Record-Shattering Launch New ‘Friday The 13th’ Movie Unveils Cast, Title & Release Date Skydance Shakes Up Cable Biz With Four Execs Running Programs & Howard Lee Exiting Par-WB Shakeup Sees Top Roles For Kira Goldberg, Erhman; Who’s Out Read More About: Comments

title: Qatar’s Film Committee Head Hassan Al-Thawadi Teases 2nd Industry Days In Doha: “We Are moving From Vision To Execution”
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Vin Diesel To Star In Action Pic 'Burial Hill'; Amazon Closing Big Deal Read the full story By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Qatar’s Film Committee Head Hassan Al-Thawadi Teases 2nd Industry Days In Doha: “We Are moving From Vision To Execution” Jean-Pierre & Luc Dardenne Set For European Film Academy Lifetime Achievement Award Festival In Focus: Qatar Ramps Up International Film & TV Ambitions As Local Talent Shines View All November 18, 2026 4:53am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Hassan Al-Thawadi Film Committee in Qatar Qatar ’s Film Committee, the body overseeing the development of the country’s film and TV business, is gearing up for the second edition of its Industry Days, running from November 19 to 20 alongside the Doha Film Festival . The inaugural edition unveiled long-gestated plans with a bang last year. Alongside a 50% film and TV cash rebate, the event also announced plans to shoot a contemporary Barbara Broccoli-produced version of Othello starring David Oyelowo and Cynthia Erivo in the Gulf state as well as partnerships with Neon, Company 3, Miramax, Department M and Sony. Related Stories News Festival In Focus: Qatar Ramps Up International Film & TV Ambitions As Local Talent Shines News Festival In Focus: Doha Gears Up For Lift-Off Against Geopolitical Odds: "It's Not Smaller, We Have More Films & Guests" On the eve of Industry Days, Hassan Al-Thawadi , Chair of the Film Committee at Media City Qatar and chief architect of its strategy, gives Deadline an update on what happened since and teases the upcoming event. Watch on Deadline DEADLINE: What was the feedback after the first edition of the Industry days? HASSAN AL-THAWADI : The feedback around Industry Days was very encouraging. The first edition gave us an opportunity to introduce our vision for Qatar’s film industry, engage the region and hear directly from filmmakers, studios, producers and financiers. More importantly, after the event, we understood that our vision resonated with support for the ecosystem around financing, production, talent, infrastructure and access to the region we are trying to build. A year later, our focus is on demonstrating how that vision is taking shape through tangible projects, partnerships and production activity. This edition is about sharing what has moved forward and the progress we have made over the past year, what we have learned, how we have adapted, and what comes next. DEADLINE: Will this edition feature as many announcements? Can you tease any? AL-THAWADI: There will be some new announcements, but I will leave the specifics for Doha . The overall message will be very clear: we are moving from vision to execution, building on what we started last year and putting more of the pieces of that ecosystem into place. Ultimately, we are open for business. Last year was about introducing the Film Committee, our ambition to transform Qatar into a global hub for the film industry, and a new proposition for the region to create greater opportunities and international visibility for Arab cinemas. This year the emphasis is on progress and moving from ambition into activity. The clearest evidence of progress this year is a portfolio of supported films with Paper Tiger , Artou and Furie s reaching international festivals, and projects moving through creative development and production planning. You will hear more about the Qatar Screen Production Incentive and how we are extending its regional reach, about projects and talent moving into their next stages, and about partnerships becoming more practical and production focused. DEADLINE: In the interim, we’ve had the U.S.-Israel war on Iran which has had fallout across the Gulf region for business and tourism. How has this impacted your plans at the Film Committee? AL-THAWADI: We can’t escape the difficult period our region has experienced. However, the fundamentals of what we are trying to build has not changed. We have a long-term strategy to attract international production, develop Arab talent and capability and to create a stronger platform for stories from our region to reach global audiences. DEADLINE: Are companies still interested in setting up here or striking partnerships? AL-THAWADI: Absolutely. We continue to see strong interest, although I think the nature of the conversation has matured. A year ago, much of the discussion was about the proposition of Qatar. Today, the conversations are increasingly around specific projects, production activity, financing, services and access to the wider region. We are already seeing that translate into production activity through the Qatar Screen Production Incentive, alongside continued engagement with international studios and production partners. The objective is not simply to have companies establish a presence in Qatar. For us, what matters most is sustained activity: productions being made, capability being transferred, local and regional talent being developed, and commercial relationships that give companies a reason to continue investing and working here and across the region. That is what we are building, and we continue to see appetite for it. DEADLINE: Have any productions accessed the rebate? AL-THAWADI: Yes. We have pilot productions already leveraging the Qatar Screen Production Incentive. Three major production companies are currently using the programme, including a leading global streaming platform, and those productions have already created more than 500 jobs locally, while generating activity for hotels, transport, security, logistics and other suppliers. For us, the important point is that we are beginning to see the incentive translate into real production activity, jobs and opportunities within Qatar, and now we’re extending its reach. We are strengthening regional collaboration and building the infrastructure that is required for global studios to film and produce in countries across the region. DEADLINE: What’s the state of play for ‘ Othello ’? AL-THAWADI : We are still in discussions with our production partner, Eon, and look forward to sharing further developments once confirmed. DEADLINE: What’s your long-term view for Qatar’s future as a media and entertainment hub? We believe Qatar can become both a gateway and a platform that serves as regional hub for the global film and entertainment industry: a gateway connecting talent, creatives and companies from our region to global markets, and a platform where international partners can work with the talent, stories and capabilities of the Arab world. My long-term view for Qatar as a hub for the global film and entertainment industry continues to be ambitious, expansive and collaborative. Success for us is not simply how many productions shoot in Qatar. It is whether we build a sustainable ecosystem with the necessary financing, production, post-production, distribution, talent development, technology and infrastructure to create lasting cultural and economic value in Qatar and across the region. Arab storytelling remains underrepresented globally. Our goal is to help create the conditions for those stories to be developed at the highest level and reach audiences around the world, while at the same time making Qatar a serious and trusted destination for international production. One of the lessons of the World Cup is that when you invest with a clear long-term purpose, you can build capability and create a legacy that extends far beyond the event itself. Film has that same ability to bring people together and broaden representation.
